result.title: The Tower of Babel in artificial intelligence: who should speak, and when it pays to listen
result.summary: Two machines can each recognize an object well and still fail together. We study classifiers that see different parts of one object and send short messages to a receiver that identifies its class. Coordination asks how to design messages together; cooperation asks whether the team outperforms one sender given the whole budget. On three digit datasets, messages designed together beat messages designed apart by 18.07 to 22.68 percentage points on average with two-bit messages, with gains in all 24 configurations. A fixed agreement, you report the row and I the column, recovers about half this gain, with only the receiver learned. Senders that draw the same distinctions waste a narrow vocabulary, and senders whose distinctions cross multiply it. A team has no more possible messages than one sender with the same budget, so a partner must bring evidence the first lacks. A solvable model shows individual statistics alone cannot determine whether a partnership helps. On MNIST digits, six shared bits remove 49.54 percent of the strongest tested solo's errors on average. Paired measurements correctly predicted most sensor teams would reduce average accuracy on new participants. Who should speak is a property of the pair, and must be measured in pairs.

AI.brief_summary: 论文研究多个只看到物体不同局部的分类器用短消息协作识别类别，比较「消息联合设计」与「各自设计」的差异，并在三个数字数据集与 MNIST 上量化团队相对单个全预算分类器的准确率收益与传感器组队效果。
AI.relevance_reason: 其「有限消息预算下伙伴必须带来首个观察者所缺的互补证据、收益只能在成对比较中测定」的框架，可能为 LVR 中何时再执行一次 LOOK、如何筛选互补视觉证据及评估其因果贡献提供概念参考，可供核查。
